title: Setting a Boundary With a Grieving Parent
script: Halimah: [thoughtful] Rizky, I need to vent for a second. My mother called four times yesterday, each time about something that genuinely could have waited until our regular Sunday visit.
Rizky: That sounds exhausting. Is this a recent shift, or has it always been this frequent?
Halimah: [carefully] It's escalated considerably since my father passed last year. I understand the loneliness underneath it, truly, but I'm struggling under the sheer volume of it.
Rizky: Understanding the cause doesn't obligate you to absorb unlimited demands, though. Those are two separate things, even if guilt tries convincing you otherwise.
Halimah: [reflective] I know that, logically. Practically, every time I consider setting a boundary, I picture her sitting alone in that house, and the whole plan dissolves instantly.
Rizky: What if the boundary wasn't about reducing contact, but restructuring it, so she gets consistency rather than whatever crisis prompts a call that particular day?
Rizky: A scheduled call every evening, say fifteen minutes, that she can actually rely on, paired with an honest conversation that spontaneous calls during work hours aren't sustainable for you.
Halimah: [gently] That's genuinely appealing, though I worry she'll interpret any structure as rejection rather than care, given how raw everything still is for her.
Rizky: Grief does distort interpretation, that's fair, but indefinitely absorbing unlimited demands isn't actually protecting her from that grief, it's just quietly depleting you instead.
Halimah: [calmly] You're right. I think I've been treating my own exhaustion as somehow selfish to even mention, as though her loss automatically disqualifies my limits.
Rizky: Her loss is real, and so are your limits. Neither cancels out the other, however much guilt insists otherwise.
Halimah: [encouraging] Okay. I'll propose the evening call this weekend, gently, and explain why, rather than just withdrawing and letting her wonder what changed.
Rizky: That honesty will likely land better than she expects. People usually sense withdrawal faster than they accept a stated boundary.
Halimah: [seriously] Thank you for saying this plainly instead of just telling me what I wanted to hear.
Rizky: That's what this is for. You'd do exactly the same for me.

quiz.question: Why has Halimah's mother been calling so frequently?
options: She needs financial help
She is moving to a new house
She is upset with Halimah
The calls have escalated since Halimah's father passed away last year
quiz.explanation: Halimah explains the calls have escalated considerably since her father passed away last year.

quiz.question: What distinction does Rizky draw between understanding the cause and absorbing demands?
options: Understanding the cause doesn't obligate absorbing unlimited demands — those are separate
They are the same thing
Only family members need to understand causes
Boundaries are never necessary with grieving parents
quiz.explanation: Rizky says understanding the cause doesn't obligate her to absorb unlimited demands; those are two separate things.

quiz.question: What alternative does Rizky suggest instead of simply reducing contact?
options: Cutting off contact entirely
Restructuring contact into a scheduled, reliable evening call
Ignoring the calls completely
Moving in with her mother
quiz.explanation: Rizky suggests a scheduled evening call she can rely on, paired with honesty that spontaneous work-hour calls aren't sustainable.

quiz.question: What does Rizky say about absorbing unlimited demands indefinitely?
options: It isn't protecting her mother from grief, it's just quietly depleting Halimah
It genuinely protects her mother from grief
It has no effect on either of them
It is the only respectful option
quiz.explanation: Rizky says indefinitely absorbing unlimited demands isn't protecting her mother from grief, it's just quietly depleting Halimah.

quiz.question: What does Halimah decide to do by the end of the conversation?
options: Say nothing and continue as before
Stop speaking to her mother entirely
Propose the evening call this weekend and explain her reasoning honestly
Ask Rizky to talk to her mother instead
quiz.explanation: Halimah decides to propose the evening call this weekend, gently, and explain why rather than simply withdrawing.

quiz.question: What distinction does Rizky make about the mother's grief?
options: Grief makes every request reasonable.
Its cause is understandable, but demands still need limits.
Boundaries are evidence of rejection.
Loneliness can be solved by avoidance.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports its cause is understandable, but demands still need limits.

quiz.question: Why is a scheduled evening call proposed?
options: It reduces all contact with the mother.
It replaces honesty with silence.
It makes grief end quickly.
It offers reliable contact while protecting work hours.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports it offers reliable contact while protecting work hours.

quiz.question: What concern makes the speaker hesitate to set structure?
options: The calls are too brief.
The speaker dislikes evenings.
The mother may misread care as rejection.
The family rejects routine.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports the mother may misread care as rejection.

quiz.question: What does Rizky identify as the cost of unlimited availability?
options: It makes the mother more independent.
It prevents any communication.
It proves stronger loyalty.
It depletes the caregiver without resolving grief.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports it depletes the caregiver without resolving grief.

quiz.question: Why is stated honesty preferred to gradual withdrawal?
options: Silence avoids every misunderstanding.
People often notice withdrawal before accepting a boundary.
Grief removes the need for explanation.
Boundaries should remain secret.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports people often notice withdrawal before accepting a boundary.
